message.content:
The sheer combinatorial explosion of chess is one of its most celebrated features.  In fact, the number of distinct positions that can arise in a game of chess is astronomically large.

| Quantity | Rough estimate |
|----------|----------------|
| **All possible positions** (legal + illegal) | ≈ 10^47 |
| **Legal positions only** | ≈ 10^46 |
| **Shannon number** (a lower bound on the game‑tree complexity) | ≈ 10^43 |

> *Shannon number* – named after Claude Shannon – is a conservative estimate of the number of legal positions that can arise in a game of chess.  It is often quoted as 10^43, but more recent analyses suggest that the true number of legal positions is closer to 10^46.

So, when people say “there are about 10^43 possible positions in chess,” they’re referring to the Shannon number.  If you include all theoretically possible configurations (even those that would never occur in a real game), the count climbs to roughly 10^47.  Either way, it’s a number far beyond the reach of brute‑force enumeration.
